clinicalPearls: SPG30 is caused by variants in KIF1A, which encodes a neuron-specific kinesin-3 motor protein; both autosomal recessive and de novo autosomal dominant forms are recognised.
It can present as either pure or complicated HSP, and the complicated form frequently features a peripheral sensory neuropathy.
Cerebellar signs with cerebellar atrophy on imaging and optic atrophy are characteristic complicating features.
SPG30 lies within the broader KIF1A-associated neurological disorder (KAND) spectrum, which also encompasses developmental disorders with epilepsy and hereditary sensory and autonomic neuropathy.
De novo dominant missense variants clustering in the motor (ATPase) domain tend to cause more severe disease with early intellectual disability, epilepsy and marked spasticity.
Recessive disease is often more restricted, presenting as a slowly progressive spastic paraparesis with neuropathy.
A negative family history does not exclude the diagnosis because many dominant cases arise de novo.
Nerve conduction studies revealing a sensory neuropathy alongside pyramidal signs are a useful pointer to this subtype.
reference.pathophysiology: SPG30 is caused by variants in KIF1A, which encodes kinesin family member 1A, a neuron-specific member of the kinesin-3 family. KIF1A is an ATP-dependent, microtubule plus-end-directed motor that drives fast anterograde axonal transport of synaptic vesicle precursors and dense-core vesicles from the neuronal cell body towards distal synapses. Pathogenic variants, especially missense changes within the catalytic motor/ATPase domain, impair the motor's ability to bind microtubules, hydrolyse ATP and move processively, thereby starving distal axons and synapses of essential cargo. Because the corticospinal and dorsal-column sensory axons are among the longest in the nervous system, they are disproportionately affected, producing length-dependent degeneration that manifests as spastic paraparesis with a sensory neuropathy; more disruptive de novo dominant variants additionally impair cortical, cerebellar and retinal neuron function, accounting for the severe complicated phenotypes.
additionalDifferentials: SPG10 (KIF5A-related), another motor-protein HSP that may include neuropathy
SPG3A (ATL1/atlastin-1), a common early-onset dominant HSP
Other phenotypes across the KIF1A-associated neurological disorder spectrum
Hereditary sensory and autonomic neuropathy of other genetic causes
Spinocerebellar ataxias where cerebellar signs predominate
Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease when peripheral neuropathy is prominent
additionalInvestigations: Nerve conduction studies and electromyography for sensory (and motor) neuropathy
MRI of the brain assessing cerebellar and optic pathway atrophy
Molecular analysis of KIF1A, interpreting variants in light of possible de novo occurrence
Broad HSP or neurodevelopmental gene panel where the phenotype is complicated
Electroencephalography where seizures form part of the presentation
redFlags: Seizures or an epileptic encephalopathy suggesting a severe dominant KAND phenotype
Developmental regression rather than the expected slow progression
Progressive visual loss from optic atrophy
Rapidly worsening ataxia indicating significant cerebellar involvement
reference.prognosis: The course is highly variable: recessive and pure forms tend to progress slowly with disability accruing over years, whereas severe de novo dominant variants with early epilepsy, intellectual disability and marked spasticity carry a worse functional outlook.
pitfalls: Considering only recessive inheritance and missing de novo dominant variants, which are a major cause
Under-recognising the breadth of the KIF1A-associated neurological disorder spectrum
Confusing SPG30 with the related motor-protein HSP SPG10 (KIF5A)
Attributing the sensory neuropathy to an unrelated acquired cause
references: Bradley and Daroff's Neurology in Clinical Practice
Adams and Victor's Principles of Neurology
GeneReviews: Hereditary Spastic Paraplegia Overview and KIF1A-Related Disorders
management: No gene-directed therapy exists; treat spasticity with oral antispasticity agents such as baclofen or tizanidine and focal botulinum toxin, with intrathecal baclofen for severe tone
Physiotherapy, stretching, orthoses and rehabilitation to maintain mobility and prevent contractures
Antiseizure medication for the epilepsy of severe de novo dominant disease
Developmental, educational and neuropsychological support for intellectual disability
Ophthalmology and low-vision support for optic atrophy, with podiatry for the sensory neuropathy
Genetic counselling addressing both recessive inheritance and de novo dominant occurrence with possible gonadal mosaicism, using parental and cascade KIF1A testing
Escalate to multidisciplinary paediatric neurology for severe early-onset KIF1A-associated phenotypes
